narrative:
Based on your profile, the model estimates a 57% chance you will not pass this year. That means, in the model’s view, failure is slightly more likely than success, which is why the remedial courses are being required. This is not a certainty, but it is a clear warning sign.

The single strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure is that you have one prior course failure. Among students who ultimately passed, the average number of past failures was zero, so having a failure already on your record stands out as a meaningful risk. This does not mean you are doomed—it simply tells the model that past difficulties may still be affecting your preparation or confidence.

The second most influential factor is your mother’s education level, which is primary school. Among students who passed, only about one in seven had a mother with this background, while the majority had mothers with more education. This is not a judgment of your ability or your family’s support. The model sees it as a general pattern: students whose parents have less formal schooling sometimes face extra challenges navigating academic demands, such as less help with homework or fewer connections to tutoring resources.

Interestingly, one factor actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing: your family relationships are good. Many successful students also report good family relationships, and this support network likely gives you emotional stability and encouragement.

To improve your chances, focus directly on your past failure. Identify what went wrong, seek extra help early, and use the remedial courses to rebuild your foundation. Your family’s support is a real strength—lean on them while you work to change this prediction.
